teile.einleitung: A clock-face timetable is a timetable in which trains and buses leave at regular intervals, always at the same minute. In 1982 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce a nationwide clock-face timetable. Since then, many departure times have been easy to remember.
wichtigste: In a clock-face timetable, trains run regularly, always at the same minute.
Switzerland introduced the nationwide clock-face timetable in 1982.
The idea came from a group of young experts who called themselves the “Spinnerclub” (crackpots’ club).
A hub is a station where trains meet so that people can change.
Bern is an important full hub in the Swiss clock-face timetable.
PostBus was also brought into the timetable pattern.
For travellers, the departure times are easy to remember.

abschnitte.text: In a **clock-face timetable**, a train leaves, for example, every hour at the same minute, such as at 7.04, 8.04 and 9.04. With a **half-hourly service**, a train comes every 30 minutes: after 7.04 the next one leaves at 7.34. In big cities, S-Bahn trains often even run every quarter of an hour. This means you do not have to look at the timetable every time.

At the beginning of the 1970s, a group of young engineers and transport experts developed the idea of a nationwide clock-face timetable. Because many people thought their plans were crazy at the time, they called themselves the **Spinnerclub**, which means something like crackpots’ club. They showed that regular connections would get more people to travel by train. Their idea was taken up by SBB.

On 23 May 1982 the nationwide **clock-face timetable** came into force in Switzerland. Most lines got at least an hourly service. Private railways and **PostBus** were also brought into the pattern so that the connections in the villages would fit. As a result, many lines got far more connections than before.

The **hubs** are especially clever. In stations such as Bern, Zurich or Basel, many trains arrive shortly before the full or half hour and leave again shortly afterwards. In a **full hub** such as Bern, trains from all directions meet in this way, and you can change easily. For this to work, the journey times between the hubs have to fit exactly.

With the **Rail 2000** project, which voters approved in 1987, the clock-face timetable was expanded further. New lines such as the new line between Mattstetten and Rothrist shortened journey times so that the hubs would work. Since 2004, trains have run every half hour on many main lines. Today other countries such as Austria and Germany take the Swiss clock-face timetable as a model.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regular gap in time at which trains or buses run.
A station where trains meet at the same time so that people can change.
A link where you can change from one train to the next.
A big expansion project of the Swiss railways for faster and more frequent connections.

gewusst: The Swiss railways are among the most punctual in the world, which is very important for connections to work in the clock-face timetable.
With Rail 2000, the journey time between Zurich and Bern was cut to just under an hour so that both hubs fit together.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Plasma Center is a research institute at EPFL, the federal institute of technology in Lausanne, which researches nuclear fusion. There, experts study how extremely hot gas, a so-called plasma, can be held in place with magnets. The aim is one day to produce energy the way the Sun does.
wichtigste: The Swiss Plasma Center is at EPFL in Lausanne.
Until 2015 it was called the Centre de Recherches en Physique des Plasmas (CRPP).
The predecessor institute has been part of EPFL since 1973.
The TCV tokamak has been in operation since 1992.
The special strength of the TCV is that it can create a great many different plasma shapes.
In 2022 researchers, together with Google DeepMind, managed to control the plasma in the TCV magnetically using artificial intelligence.
Superconducting cables for fusion magnets are tested in the SULTAN facility at the PSI in Villigen.

abschnitte.text: In the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones and release huge amounts of energy as they do so. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. On Earth, it needs temperatures of more than 100 million degrees. At such heat, gas turns into a **plasma**, in which electrons and atomic nuclei move about freely.

A plasma this hot must not touch any wall, so it is held in a ring-shaped vessel by strong magnetic fields. Such a machine is called a **tokamak**. Since 1992 the Swiss Plasma Center has run the **TCV**, the Tokamak à configuration variable. Its strength is that it can create a great many different plasma shapes, which makes it special worldwide.

At the TCV, for example, the **snowflake divertor** was studied, a special magnetic field shape that looks like a snowflake. A divertor carries hot particles away from the plasma and so protects the walls. In 2022 researchers from the Swiss Plasma Center, together with **Google DeepMind**, managed to control the plasma magnetically using **artificial intelligence**. The program learnt to adjust the magnetic coils so that the plasma took on the desired shape.

Large fusion machines need very strong magnets made of **superconductors**, which conduct electricity without resistance when they are strongly cooled. For this, the Swiss Plasma Center runs the **SULTAN** test facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in Aargau. There, superconducting cables are tested under extreme conditions. Cables for the international experimental reactor ITER in France were also tested here.

The institute used to be called the **Centre de Recherches en Physique des Plasmas**, CRPP for short, and has been part of EPFL since 1973. Since 2015 it has had the name Swiss Plasma Center. It is the most important centre for fusion research in Switzerland and works closely with research groups all over Europe. Many young physicists are also trained there.

begriffe.erklaerung: An extremely hot gas in which electrons and atomic nuclei are separated.
The fusing of atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
A ring-shaped machine that holds plasma in place with magnetic fields.
A material that, when cooled, conducts electricity with no resistance at all.

gewusst: The plasma in a tokamak is many times hotter than the inside of the Sun.
The word tokamak comes from Russian, because this design was invented in the Soviet Union.

teile.einleitung: A jet engine is an aircraft engine that sucks in air, burns it with fuel and pushes it out backwards as a hot jet. This pushes the aircraft forwards. Almost all large passenger aircraft and fighter jets fly with such engines today.
wichtigste: The thrust of a jet engine is based on the principle of recoil.
In 1930 Frank Whittle applied for a patent for a turbojet engine in Great Britain.
In 1939 the Heinkel He 178 was the first aircraft to fly with a turbine jet engine.
A turbofan sends a large part of the air past the hot core.
Accelerating a lot of air a little is more economical than accelerating a little air a lot.
A ramjet has no compressor and only works at high speed.
An afterburner gives fighter aircraft more thrust but uses much more fuel.

abschnitte.text: If you let go of a blown-up balloon, the air shoots out at the back and the balloon flies forwards. A jet engine works in exactly the same way, using the **principle of recoil**. The more air per second is accelerated backwards and the faster it comes out, the greater the **thrust**. If an engine accelerates, for example, 50 kilograms of air per second from 250 to 650 metres per second, this gives roughly 20 kilonewtons of thrust.

At the front, the **intake** sucks in the air. The **compressor** squeezes it together strongly with many bladed wheels. In the **combustion chamber**, kerosene is injected and burnt, which makes the gases very hot so that they expand. They drive a turbine, which in turn spins the compressor, and then flow out backwards through the nozzle.

Modern airliners have **turbofan engines** with a huge fan at the front. Most of the air flows past the hot core and produces most of the thrust. The **bypass ratio** tells you how much air flows past the core compared with the air that goes through the core. The higher it is, the more economical and quieter the engine.

In 1930 the Briton **Frank Whittle** applied for a patent for a turbojet engine. In Germany, Hans von Ohain developed his own engine independently. With it, on 27 August 1939, the **Heinkel He 178** became the first aircraft in the world to fly with turbine jet propulsion. After the Second World War, jet engines quickly took over in aviation.

A **ramjet** has no mechanical compressor. The air is squeezed together only by the high flying speed, so it only works once the aircraft is already very fast. Fighter aircraft often have an **afterburner**, which burns extra fuel behind the turbine. This gives much more thrust at take-off or in supersonic flight, but costs a great deal more fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which an engine pushes an aircraft forwards.
A part with bladed wheels that squeezes the air that has been sucked in.
A bladed wheel that is driven by flowing gas.
How much air flows past the engine core compared with the air that goes through the core.

gewusst: In modern passenger jets, often ten times more air flows past the core than through it.
The combustion chamber of an engine is hotter than the metals of the turbine blades can actually withstand, so they are cooled with air.

teile.einleitung: Streaming means that music or videos are played over the internet while the data is still loading. So you do not have to wait until a whole file has been downloaded. Music services, video platforms and livestreams all work on this principle.
wichtigste: With streaming you play music or videos while the data is still loading.
A buffer loads a few seconds in advance so that playback does not stutter.
Videos are compressed so that less data has to be sent.
The bitrate tells you how much data is sent per second.
With slow internet, the picture quality adjusts automatically and becomes blurrier.
A livestream broadcasts an event in real time.
With a download, a file is saved permanently; with streaming it usually is not.

abschnitte.text: The English word **stream** means a current or a brook. With streaming, the data flows without a break from the server to the device, like a brook. The video or song starts after a few seconds, even though far from everything has arrived yet. Unlike with a **download**, the file normally does not stay saved on the device afterwards.

So that it does not keep juddering, the device always loads a few seconds ahead into a temporary store, the **buffer**. If the internet slows down for a moment, the buffer is used up first. The **bitrate** tells you how much data is sent per second. A video in high resolution needs a much higher bitrate than a song.

An uncompressed video would be huge and could hardly be sent. That is why it is **compressed**: a program leaves out information that you would hardly notice, for example parts of the picture that do not change from one frame to the next. With **adaptive streaming**, several quality levels are ready. If the connection is slow, the player automatically switches to a blurrier version so that the video keeps playing.

Big providers do not store their videos in just one place. They use **content delivery networks**, which are networks of many servers all over the world. A video then comes from a server that is as close as possible to the viewers. This makes the transfer faster and takes pressure off the internet.

In a **livestream**, an event is broadcast in real time, such as a football match, a concert or a computer game. Swiss television also offers its programmes for streaming on platforms such as Play SRF. Because streaming uses a lot of data, it is worth using wifi when you are out rather than mobile data. Data centres and data transfer also use electricity, so streaming sparingly is good for the environment too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A temporary store that loads data in advance.
The amount of data that is sent per second.
To make data smaller so that it takes up less space.
A computer on the internet that provides data for other devices.

gewusst: Video streaming makes up a large part of all the data traffic on the internet.
In a livestream the picture often arrives a few seconds later than it really happens.

teile.einleitung: Swissmetro was a bold Swiss transport project: trains were to race through Switzerland in tubes deep underground at several hundred kilometres per hour. From Bern to Zurich would have taken only about 12 minutes. Swissmetro was never built, but the idea lives on to this day.
wichtigste: Swissmetro was meant to be a maglev train in underground tubes with thin air.
The engineer Rodolphe Nieth launched the project in 1974.
The air in the tubes was to be reduced to about 10 percent of normal air pressure.
A main line was planned from Geneva via Lausanne, Bern and Zurich to St Gallen.
In 1992 Swissmetro AG was founded, and in 1998 an application for a licence for the Geneva to Lausanne line followed.
In 2009 Swissmetro AG was wound up.
The successor project Swissmetro-NG is developing the idea further.

abschnitte.text: Swissmetro was meant to connect the big Swiss cities so quickly that they would become almost like one single big city. The vehicles were not to roll on wheels but to float above the track as a **maglev train**. Speeds of about 400 to 500 kilometres per hour were planned. A journey from Bern to Zurich would then have taken only about 12 minutes, and a journey from Geneva to St Gallen less than an hour.

At high speed, **air resistance** is the biggest obstacle: it slows you down and uses a lot of energy. That is why the vehicles were to run in tunnel tubes in which the air is thinned to about 10 percent of normal air pressure, similar to the air at great flying heights. The tubes were to lie deep underground so that they would not cut through the landscape. Magnetic forces would have carried, guided and driven the vehicles.

The French-speaking Swiss engineer **Rodolphe Nieth** launched the idea in 1974. Experts, among others from EPFL in Lausanne, developed the concept further, and in 1992 **Swissmetro AG** was founded. In 1998 the promoters submitted an application for a licence for a first pilot line from Geneva to Lausanne. Because of the enormous costs and a lack of investors, however, it was never built, and in 2009 the company was wound up.

With **Swissmetro-NG** there is a successor project that is developing the idea further with new technology. Similar ideas are being studied around the world under the name **Hyperloop**, in which capsules are to travel through tubes that are almost empty of air. In Switzerland, researchers are testing on test tracks how such systems could work. Whether such a train will ever be built for passengers is still open.

begriffe.erklaerung: A train that is carried by magnets and floats above the track without wheels.
How strongly the air presses on everything; in thin air it is lower.
The force with which the air slows down a fast vehicle.
Permission from the state, for example to build and run a railway line.

gewusst: The Swissmetro idea came about almost 40 years before the term Hyperloop became known around the world.
With Swissmetro, the journey from Bern to Zurich would have been shorter than many people’s journey to work.
The tubes were to lie so deep that nothing would have been noticed at the surface.

teile.einleitung: Taylorism is a method of planning work in factories as precisely as possible and breaking it down into small, simple steps. It goes back to the American engineer Frederick Winslow Taylor, who studied work with a stopwatch around 1900. His ideas changed industry worldwide, but they were also strongly criticised.
wichtigste: In 1911 Frederick Winslow Taylor published his main work, The Principles of Scientific Management.
A key feature of Taylorism is the separation of planning work from carrying out work.
Taylor studied the individual work steps with a stopwatch in time studies.
His experiments on loading pig iron at the Bethlehem Steel works are well known.
He suggested performance-related pay with a bonus for completing the set amount of work.
Frank and Lillian Gilbreth added precise motion studies to Taylor’s time studies.
Taylorism is criticised above all for monotonous work and the loss of craft skills.

abschnitte.text: **Frederick Winslow Taylor** lived from 1856 to 1915 in the USA. In a steelworks he worked his way up from ordinary labourer to engineer. While doing so, he noticed that many jobs were done without planning and at different speeds. He wanted to find out the best way to carry out every task and called this **scientific management**.

Taylor broke every job down into small steps and measured with a **stopwatch** how long each step took. Such **time studies** showed him which movements were unnecessary. At the **Bethlehem Steel** works he studied how workers loaded heavy bars of pig iron. With fixed breaks and precise instructions, they managed many times the amount they had before.

One principle of Taylorism is the separation of **planning** work from **carrying out** work. Engineers and supervisors decide how a job is to be done and how long it should take. The workers then only carry out the set movements. Anyone who completed the set amount of work was to be rewarded with **performance-related pay** and a bonus.

Taylor’s book **The Principles of Scientific Management** appeared in 1911 and was translated into many languages. The married couple Frank and Lillian Gilbreth added precise **motion studies** to his time studies, filming the movements of the hands. From 1913 Henry Ford combined these ideas with the **assembly line** in car production. In Germany, the association **REFA** was founded in 1924 to standardise time studies and the design of work.

Many people criticised the fact that work became very **monotonous**, because you made the same movement all day long. The craftsmen’s expertise and skill were lost, and the pressure on the workers increased. Charlie Chaplin’s film Modern Times from 1936 makes fun of this kind of work. Today many companies rely more on teamwork and varied tasks, but time measurement and precise planning are still common in industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measuring exactly how long a work step takes.
A conveyor belt on which a product moves from one workstation to the next.
Pay that depends on how much someone gets done.
Sameness, when you do the same thing over and over again.

gewusst: Taylor was also a good sportsman and, together with a partner, won the US doubles championship in tennis in 1881.
The Gilbreths had twelve children, and their family life was later told in the book and film Cheaper by the Dozen.

teile.einleitung: SwissFEL is an X-ray laser at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. It produces extremely short and bright flashes of X-ray light. With them, researchers can watch how atoms and molecules move in tiny fractions of a second.
wichtigste: SwissFEL is a free-electron X-ray laser at the Paul Scherrer Institute.
The facility is about 740 metres long in total.
SwissFEL was inaugurated in 2016.
The electrons are accelerated to an energy of about 5.8 GeV.
In an undulator, a row of magnets with alternating poles, the electrons give off X-ray light.
The X-ray pulses last only a few femtoseconds.
The Aramis beamline delivers hard X-rays.
SwissFEL can produce up to 100 X-ray pulses per second.

abschnitte.text: A **free-electron laser**, FEL for short, does not produce light with crystals or gases like other lasers. Instead, **electrons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Then they are sent through a long row of magnets, where they give off extremely bright X-ray light. SwissFEL is one of the largest research facilities in Switzerland.

First, in a building about 740 metres long, electrons are brought to an energy of about 5.8 GeV in a **linear accelerator**. Then they fly through the **undulator**, an arrangement of magnets with alternating poles. There they are steered back and forth like a slalom skier and give off X-ray light as they go. The light amplifies itself, so that a very bright, laser-like flash is produced.

The X-ray pulses last only a few **femtoseconds**. A femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second. In this time, even light travels only a fraction of the thickness of a hair. SwissFEL can produce up to 100 such pulses per second.

SwissFEL has two beamlines. **Aramis** delivers hard X-rays, which can make very fine structures such as the arrangement of atoms visible. **Athos** delivers softer X-rays, which are suitable, for example, for studying magnetic materials and chemical reactions. Researchers from all over the world work at the experiment stations.

With the short flashes, you can take snapshots, rather like with a high-speed camera. If you put many pictures in a row, you get a kind of **molecular film** that shows how a chemical reaction takes place. In this way scientists can study, for example, how plants use light for photosynthesis or how medicines attach to proteins. There are only a few similar facilities in the world, for example the European XFEL in Hamburg.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row of magnets that forces electrons onto a wavy path.
A quadrillionth of a second, so unimaginably short.
A straight facility in which particles are made faster and faster.
Invisible, very high-energy light that can pass into materials.

gewusst: The abbreviation FEL stands for free-electron laser.
An X-ray pulse from SwissFEL is so short that, compared with one second, it is about as long as one second compared with several million years.

teile.einleitung: Electricity consumption tells you how much electrical energy appliances, households or a whole country need. It is usually measured in kilowatt hours. If you know which appliances use a lot of electricity, you can save energy and money.
wichtigste: On the electricity bill, consumption is given in kilowatt hours (kWh).
In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 terawatt hours of electricity (final consumption).
Electricity consumption in Switzerland is highest in winter.
An appliance with 2000 watts that runs for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
The energy label shows how economical an appliance is with energy.
Even appliances that seem to be switched off still use electricity on standby.
LED lamps use less electricity than light bulbs, because they turn more energy into light and less into heat.

abschnitte.text: The **power** of an appliance is given in watts; a kettle, for example, has 2000 watts. How much energy is used also depends on how long the appliance runs. You multiply power by time: 2000 watts for 3 hours gives 6000 watt hours, which is 6 **kilowatt hours**. If a kilowatt hour costs 30 centimes, these 6 kWh cost 1.80 francs altogether.

In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 **terawatt hours** of electricity, which is 57 billion kilowatt hours. About a third of this is used by households, and the rest mainly by industry, trade, services and transport, for example the railways. Most electricity is needed in **winter**, because it is dark for longer and many heat pumps are heating. At the same time, hydropower and solar panels supply less in winter, so Switzerland then imports electricity.

Fridges, washing machines and televisions carry a coloured **energy label**. It uses letters and colours from green to red to show how economical an appliance is. Green classes mean low consumption, red classes mean high consumption. When buying, an economical appliance is worth it, because it uses less electricity over many years.

Appliances that heat or cool use a lot of electricity, such as the oven, the tumble dryer, the fridge or an electric water heater. An **LED lamp** needs only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb for the same brightness. This is because a light bulb turns most of its energy into heat instead of light. The **standby consumption** of televisions, games consoles or chargers also adds up over the year.

Switching appliances off completely or using an extension lead with a switch saves standby electricity. When cooking, a lid on the pan helps, and it is best to heat water in a kettle. Switching off the light in empty rooms is an easy contribution. If you use less electricity, you save money and protect the **environment**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of energy: 1000 watts for one hour.
How much energy an appliance needs per second, measured in watts.
A ready state in which the appliance seems to be off but still uses electricity.
A sticker that shows how economical an appliance is.

gewusst: One terawatt hour is a billion kilowatt hours.
With one kilowatt hour, a 10-watt LED lamp can shine for about 100 hours.

teile.einleitung: A tram is an electrically powered rail vehicle that runs right through the streets of a town. In Switzerland people usually just say “Tram”. In Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva, trams are a firm part of the townscape.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the tram is usually called “Tram”.
A tram takes its electricity from a line above the street through a pantograph.
Because it runs on rails, a tram cannot swerve around obstacles.
A tram warns people in the street with a bell.
The trams in Zurich are blue and white, the BVB trams in Basel are green.
The first tram in Zurich was pulled by horses and was called the “Rösslitram”.
Trams have right of way, even on zebra crossings.

abschnitte.text: A **tram** runs on rails set into the street and often shares the street with cars, bikes and pedestrians. It can carry many more people than a bus and needs no fuel to do so. Modern trams have a low floor, so you can easily get on even with a pushchair or wheelchair. Because they run on electricity, they are quiet and give off no exhaust fumes in town.

Above the streets hangs an **overhead line**, a wire that carries electric current. An arm on the roof, the **pantograph**, presses against this wire from below and so collects the electricity. The current flows through the electric motors and back through the rails. In Switzerland, the city trams in Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva run on **metre gauge**, which means the rails are one metre apart.

A tram cannot swerve and, because of its great weight, needs a long distance to brake. That is why it warns with a bright **bell** when someone is standing on the rails. In Swiss road traffic the tram has right of way, even on zebra crossings. When cycling, you have to be careful that your wheel does not get caught in the grooves of the rails, and cross rails as close to a right angle as possible.

The first trams were pulled by horses; in Zurich it was called the **Rösslitram** and ran from 1882. In 1881 Werner von Siemens opened the world’s first electric tramway near Berlin. Soon the horses were replaced by electric motors in Swiss towns too, in Zurich from 1894. Many Swiss towns removed their tram networks in the 20th century, but Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva kept them and are expanding them again today.

The blue and white trams of the Zurich transport company, VBZ, form the largest tram network in Switzerland. In Basel, the green trams of the **BVB** and the yellow trams of the BLT run, and some lines even go as far as Germany and France. Bern has red trams run by Bernmobil, and in Geneva the trams of the TPG run. Newer lines such as the Glattalbahn and the Limmattalbahn now also connect suburbs with the city.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rail vehicle that runs through the streets; in Switzerland this is the usual word.
A wire above the street from which the tram gets its electricity.
An arm on the roof that collects electricity from the overhead line.
Rails that are one metre apart.

gewusst: With the Basel tram you can cross the national border as far as Weil am Rhein in Germany.
One long tram can carry as many people at once as several buses together.
The word “tram” comes from English and originally meant a rail or a wagon in mines.

teile.einleitung: A barcode is a pattern of dark bars and light gaps in which a number is hidden. A scanner can read this number in a fraction of a second. Almost every product in a shop carries a barcode, so that the till knows straight away what it is and how much it costs.
wichtigste: The EAN barcode on most products has 13 digits.
The last digit is a check digit, which is used to spot reading errors.
Companies with numbers from Switzerland have barcodes that begin with 760 to 769.
Books carry a barcode with the ISBN, which begins with 978 or 979.
Dark bars reflect less light than light gaps, so the scanner can tell them apart.
Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver patented the idea in 1952.
A barcode is one-dimensional, a QR code is two-dimensional.

abschnitte.text: A barcode contains a coded number that clearly identifies the product. The best-known form is the **EAN code** with 13 digits, which are also printed below the bars. The first digits show in which country the company received its number; for Switzerland and Liechtenstein these are 760 to 769. Then come numbers for the company and the product, and right at the end is the **check digit**.

abschnitte.titel: How does the scanner read it?
abschnitte.text: A **scanner** lights up the barcode with a beam of light or records it with a camera. The dark bars swallow a lot of light, while the light gaps reflect it. From the pattern of wide and narrow bars, the device works out the number. Using the check digit, the computer checks immediately whether it has been read correctly.

At the till, the computer looks up the price and the name of the product for that number. This way the shop can also keep exact track of how many packs are still in stock. But you also find barcodes on parcels, library books, train tickets or luggage tags at the airport. On books, the barcode contains the **ISBN**, which begins with 978 or 979.

The idea comes from the Americans **Norman Joseph Woodland** and **Bernard Silver**, who were granted a patent for it in 1952. Woodland is said to have had the idea while drawing Morse code in the sand with his fingers and stretching the dots and dashes downwards. In 1974, a product was scanned at a till for the first time, in a supermarket in the USA. It was a packet of chewing gum.

A normal barcode is read in one direction only, from left to right, so it is **one-dimensional**. A **QR code**, on the other hand, is made of small squares and stores information in two directions. That is why much more fits into a QR code, for example an internet address or a whole text. In Switzerland, the QR code is used, for example, on the QR bill for paying.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for an article number with 13 digits that is used worldwide.
A calculated last digit that is used to detect reading errors.
A number that clearly identifies every book.
A reading device that recognises barcodes using light.

gewusst: The packet of chewing gum that was the first to be scanned in 1974 is now in a museum in the USA.
The country number in the barcode only shows where the company is registered, not where the product was made.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit is a closed path along which electric current flows from a power source to a device and back again. Only if this circuit is not broken anywhere does a lamp light up or a motor run. There are circuits in every torch, in every battery-powered toy and in every house.
wichtigste: For a lamp to light up on a battery, you need a closed circuit.
If you undo a wire, the circuit is broken and the lamp goes out.
Metals such as copper conduct electricity well.
Materials such as rubber, plastic or glass do not let electricity through; they are called insulators.
If two small bulbs are connected one after the other and one is unscrewed, both go out.
The fuse in the house switches off the electricity if too much current flows.
A yellow warning triangle with a black lightning bolt warns of danger from electricity.

abschnitte.text: A simple circuit has a **power source**, for example a battery. Then there is something that uses the power, such as a small bulb, and wires that connect everything together. Often there is also a **switch**, with which you can open and close the circuit. You can imagine the current like water being pumped round in a loop through pipes.

Current only flows when the circuit is **closed**. If you undo a wire or open the switch, the path is broken and the lamp goes out immediately. A light switch on the wall does exactly that: it opens or closes a circuit. If two wires in a circuit touch each other directly, without a device in between, a dangerous **short circuit** occurs.

Metals such as **copper**, aluminium or iron conduct electricity well, which is why cables are made of copper wire inside. Materials such as rubber, plastic, wood or glass, on the other hand, do not conduct electricity. They are called **insulators**. The plastic coating of a cable protects us from touching the current.

In a **series circuit**, several small bulbs are connected one after the other in a single loop. If you unscrew one, the circuit is broken and all of them go out. In a **parallel circuit**, each bulb has its own path to the battery. If one fails, the others stay lit; this is also how the lights in a flat are connected.

abschnitte.titel: Electricity at home and in nature
abschnitte.text: At home, the **fuse** in the fuse box protects the wiring: if too much current flows, it switches off. Electricity from a socket is much stronger than that from a battery and can be deadly. A yellow warning triangle with a black lightning bolt shows that there is danger from electricity. In nature there are huge electric sparks during a **thunderstorm**, which we see as lightning.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that supplies electricity, for example a battery.
A material through which electricity can flow easily.
A material that does not let electricity through.
When current flows straight back without a device, which can get dangerously hot.

gewusst: With a lemon, a piece of copper and a galvanised nail you can build a small battery.
Our bodies conduct electricity too, so you must never fiddle with sockets or power lines.

teile.einleitung: Sulzer is an industrial company with a long tradition from Winterthur, which started in 1834 as a small iron foundry. In the 19th and 20th centuries it became world-famous for steam engines, huge ship engines and weaving machines. Today Sulzer concentrates mainly on pumps and flow technology.
wichtigste: Sulzer started in 1834 in Winterthur with an iron foundry.
For a long time the company was called Gebrüder Sulzer (Sulzer Brothers).
In the 1880s Sulzer had great international success with steam engines.
In 1881 Sulzer opened its first branch factory in Ludwigshafen in Germany.
Large two-stroke diesel engines made Sulzer world-famous in shipbuilding.
From the 1950s, the projectile weaving machine became an export success.
The large-engine business is carried on today by WinGD (Winterthur Gas & Diesel).
Today Sulzer concentrates mainly on pumps and flow technology (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: In 1834 the Sulzer family founded an **iron foundry** in **Winterthur**. Johann Jakob Sulzer ran the business together with his sons, which is why the company was called **Gebrüder Sulzer** (Sulzer Brothers) for a long time. At first they cast parts from iron, but soon they were building whole machines. With Sulzer and other firms, Winterthur grew into an important industrial town.

In the 19th century Sulzer made **steam engines**, which powered factories, pumps and ships. Sulzer engines were considered especially economical and reliable. In the 1880s they were sold to many countries. In 1881 Sulzer opened its first branch factory in **Ludwigshafen** in Germany.

At the end of the 19th century Sulzer worked with the inventor Rudolf Diesel and soon built its own **diesel engines**. The huge **two-stroke diesel engines** that power large cargo ships and tankers became famous. Such engines are as big as a house with several storeys. Today this business is carried on in Winterthur by the company **WinGD** (Winterthur Gas & Diesel).

From the 1950s Sulzer built the **projectile weaving machine**. In this machine, a small piece of metal, the projectile, shoots the thread across through the cloth instead of a heavy shuttle. The machine was fast and efficient and was exported to many countries. Sulzer also made heating systems, refrigeration plants and medical products.

From the 1980s Sulzer sold many of its business areas and reorganised itself greatly. Today the company concentrates mainly on **pumps** and **flow technology**, for instance for water supply, chemicals or energy (as of 2025). Its headquarters are still in Winterthur. On the former factory site in the centre of Winterthur there are now flats, schools, offices and cultural venues.

begriffe.erklaerung: A works where liquid iron is poured into moulds.
A combustion engine that fires once with every turn.
Here a small piece of metal that carries the thread through the weaving machine.
Technology that moves liquids and gases, for example with pumps.

gewusst: As a young engineer, Rudolf Diesel worked for a short time at Sulzer in Winterthur, and Sulzer was later one of the first companies to build his engine under licence.
A large ship’s diesel engine in the Sulzer tradition can have more power than hundreds of car engines together.

teile.einleitung: A signal box is the control centre of the railway, where points and signals are set and secured. It makes sure that every train runs on the right track and that no trains collide. In the past, heavy levers were moved to do this; today computers usually do the job.
wichtigste: A signal box sets and secures points and signals.
In the signal box, the train dispatcher controls the train traffic.
In old mechanical signal boxes, points and signals were moved with levers and wires.
A relay signal box works with many electrical switches called relays.
Modern electronic signal boxes work with computers.
The secured route of a train through a station is called a route.
SBB controls its traffic from large operations centres, one of which is in Olten.

abschnitte.titel: The job of a signal box
abschnitte.text: A train cannot steer; it always follows the rails. Whether it goes left or right is decided by the **points**. Whether it may go or has to stop is shown by the **signals**. The signal box controls both and constantly checks that everything fits together.

For every train, a particular path through the station is set: the **route**. Only when all the points are in the right position and locked can the signal be set to go. This safety technology prevents a signal from showing green while a set of points is in the wrong position. In addition, no second route can be set that crosses or endangers the first one.

The first signal boxes appeared in the 19th century. In a **mechanical signal box** there were long rows of heavy levers. Using **wires** and rods, the signalman moved the points and signals, which were often hundreds of metres away. This was hard physical work, and every larger station needed its own staff.

In the 20th century, electrical signal boxes came in. A **relay signal box** secures the routes with thousands of small electrical switches, the relays. In Switzerland, track-diagram signal boxes were especially common, in which the track layout is reproduced on a control desk. Today more and more **electronic signal boxes** are being built, in which computers take over the safety functions.

In the past, almost every station had its own signal box with staff on site. Today SBB controls its network from four large **operations centres** in Lausanne, Olten, Pollegio and Zurich Airport. There, train dispatchers monitor long stretches of line on many screens. The signal boxes in the stations are operated remotely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where the track divides, used to send a train onto another track.
The set and secured path for a train.
An electrical switch that is operated by electric current.
The person who controls the train traffic in an area.

gewusst: Some old mechanical signal boxes can be visited today as museums.
A single modern signal box can control points and signals over many kilometres of line and in several stations.

teile.einleitung: A superalloy is a particularly tough metal material that stays strong even at very high temperatures. Most superalloys consist mainly of nickel, mixed with other metals. Without them there would be no modern aircraft engines or gas turbines.
wichtigste: Most superalloys for turbine blades are based on nickel.
Besides nickel, there are also superalloys based on cobalt.
The finely distributed gamma prime phase Ni₃Al is mainly responsible for the high strength at high temperatures.
Creep is the name for the slow, permanent deformation under load at high temperature.
Turbine blades are often cast as a single crystal, because without grain boundaries they deform more slowly.
The blades are usually made by vacuum investment casting.
A ceramic thermal barrier coating made of zirconium oxide and fine cooling channels protect the blades as well.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is a mixture of several metals, like bronze, which is made from copper and tin. Superalloys usually consist mostly of **nickel** and also contain chromium, aluminium, cobalt and other elements. There are also superalloys based on **cobalt**. Their special feature is that they stay very strong even close to their melting point.

Normal metals become soft when they are very hot. Under constant load they then stretch very slowly, like chewing gum being pulled apart. This slow, permanent deformation is called **creep**. In an engine, the turbine blades spin very fast in hot gases, so they have to resist creep particularly well.

Under the microscope, you can see tiny little cubes of a compound of nickel and aluminium in a nickel-based superalloy. This **gamma prime phase**, with the formula Ni₃Al, is finely distributed in the metal. It blocks the movements in the crystal lattice that would otherwise deform the metal. This keeps the material strong even in great heat.

Normal metals are made of many small crystal grains, with **grain boundaries** between them. It is precisely at these boundaries that the metal starts to creep in the heat. That is why highly stressed turbine blades are cast as a **single crystal**, that is, from one single continuous crystal. They are made by **vacuum investment casting**, in which the metal flows into a ceramic mould with no air present and solidifies in a controlled way.

The gases in an engine are often hotter than the melting point of the blades. That is why the blades have fine **cooling channels** inside, through which air from the compressor flows. On the outside, a thin ceramic **thermal barrier coating** based on zirconium oxide protects them. Superalloys are used in aircraft engines, in gas turbines in power stations and in rockets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal with other elements.
Slow, permanent deformation of a material under load in the heat.
A workpiece that consists of one single continuous crystal.
A very precise casting method using ceramic moulds.

gewusst: The first superalloys were developed in the 1940s for the early jet engines.
Without the air cooling inside, some turbine blades would melt during operation.

teile.einleitung: A socket is the connection point in the wall where you connect electrical appliances to the mains. When you push a plug into it, electricity flows to the appliance. Because a dangerous voltage of 230 volts is present in the socket, you have to be very careful with it.
wichtigste: A normal Swiss socket has three holes for a plug.
A Swiss socket carries a voltage of 230 volts.
You must never push objects such as needles or scissors into a socket.
Child safety covers stop children from pushing things into it.
You should never plug in appliances with wet hands, because water can conduct electricity.
When unplugging, you always hold the plug and never pull on the cable.
Only a qualified electrician may connect new sockets.

abschnitte.text: A socket connects appliances such as lamps, toasters or chargers to the **mains**. Inside the wall, cables run from the fuse box to the socket. When you push a plug in, the **circuit** closes and the appliance gets electricity. An **extension lead** offers several sockets on one cable.

The normal Swiss socket has three holes in a flat hexagonal shape. Two holes are for the wires that bring the electricity in and carry it back. The third is for the **earth wire**, which safely carries the current into the ground if there is a fault. The voltage is 230 **volts** at a frequency of 50 hertz.

Almost every country has its own plug shape. The thick German Schuko plug, for example, does not fit into a normal Swiss socket, and in Great Britain sockets look completely different. That is why you often need a **travel adapter** on holiday. The flat two-pin Europlug, which you find on many mobile phone chargers, does fit into many European sockets, including Swiss ones.

Electricity from a socket can be deadly. So you must never poke metal objects such as needles, scissors or screws into the holes. Many sockets have a **child safety cover**, where small flaps close the holes. Because **water** can conduct electricity, you must never plug in appliances with wet hands or near the bath.

When unplugging, you hold the plug and do not pull on the cable, otherwise the wires inside can break. You should stop using damaged cables or plugs. Only a **qualified electrician** may connect new sockets, for example an electrical installer. A residual current device in the fuse box switches off the electricity in a flash if the current takes a wrong path.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how strongly the electric current is driven, measured in volts.
A wire that carries the current away safely if there is a fault.
An in-between plug so that an appliance fits into sockets abroad.
A switch that cuts off the electricity immediately if it could flow through a person.

gewusst: Around the world there are more than a dozen different plug types, named with the letters A to N.
The Swiss plug is type J and is used almost only in Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

teile.einleitung: A torch is a small, portable lamp that shines using batteries or a rechargeable battery. It helps in the dark, when camping, in a power cut or even in an emergency in the mountains. Today almost every torch has an economical LED.
wichtigste: A torch gets its electricity from batteries or a rechargeable battery.
Most modern torches have an LED.
A shiny mirror behind the bulb directs the light forwards.
When the batteries run low, the torch shines more weakly.
With a wind-up torch you make the electricity yourself by turning a handle.
A head torch is worn on the head with a strap.
For the alpine distress signal, you give a light signal six times a minute.

abschnitte.text: In a torch, the **battery**, the switch and the bulb form a closed circuit. When you press the switch, electricity flows from the battery through the light source and it lights up. Behind the bulb there is a curved, shiny **reflector**, which focuses the light forwards like a mirror. At the front, a pane of glass or plastic protects the inside.

In the past, torches had a small light bulb that used a lot of electricity and often burnt out. Today almost always **LEDs** are used, that is light-emitting diodes, which are much brighter and need much less electricity. An LED also lasts tens of thousands of hours and is not easily damaged by knocks. How bright a torch is is given in **lumens**.

Most torches use batteries or **rechargeable batteries**, and many can now be charged with a USB cable. When the batteries run low, the voltage drops and the light gets weaker. Wind-up torches need no battery at all: a small **dynamo** inside produces electricity when you turn the handle. Empty batteries do not belong in the rubbish but back in the shop at the collection point.

A **head torch** is worn on the head with a strap, so both hands stay free when hiking, climbing or putting up a tent. There are small keyring torches, waterproof diving torches and powerful torches for the police and fire brigade. Many mobile phones have a built-in torch function. The first battery torch was built in the USA around 1900.

In the Alps you can use a torch to give the **alpine distress signal**: a light signal six times a minute, then a minute’s break. The rescuers reply with three signals a minute. A torch also belongs in the emergency supply at home, so that you have light in a power cut. You never shine a torch into anyone’s eyes, because bright light dazzles and can harm the eyes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A curved mirror that directs the light forwards.
Light-emitting diode, an economical electronic light source.
A battery that can be charged again.
A unit that measures how much light a lamp gives off.
A small generator that turns movement into electricity.

gewusst: In American English a torch is called a “flashlight”, because early torches could only give short flashes of light before the weak batteries had to recover.
Modern LED torches are often much brighter than the best torches of thirty years ago and still use less electricity.
For the alpine distress signal you can also use whistles or shouts instead of light.

teile.einleitung: In a power cut, electricity suddenly stops flowing through the lines. Lights go out, fridges get warm and often the mobile network, traffic lights and trains fail too. Usually a power cut lasts only a short time, but big outages can affect millions of people.
wichtigste: The great power cut in Italy on 28 September 2003 began with a flashover from a Swiss high-voltage line to a tree.
On 22 June 2005 the SBB railway power network failed across the whole of Switzerland for several hours.
On 28 April 2025, Spain and Portugal above all were hit by a widespread power cut.
When, after an outage, more overloaded lines switch off one after another, this is called a cascade effect.
A power station with black start capability can start up on its own without electricity from the grid.
Hospitals bridge the first seconds with an uninterruptible power supply from batteries.
In Switzerland the organisation OSTRAL prepares measures for an electricity shortage.

abschnitte.text: Power cuts happen, for example, when a storm blows trees onto lines or lightning strikes. Technical faults, diggers that damage a cable or errors in control systems can also be to blame. When one line fails, the electricity has to flow through other lines. If these become overloaded and switch off as well, a **cascade effect** occurs, spreading like dominoes.

On 28 September 2003, a high-voltage line on the Lukmanier in Switzerland came too close to a tree, and there was a **flashover**. As a result, the power failed in almost the whole of Italy. On 22 June 2005, the SBB **railway power network** collapsed across the whole of Switzerland, and in the middle of the evening rush hour many trains came to a standstill. On 28 April 2025, Spain and Portugal were almost completely without electricity.

Grid operators plan their network according to the **(n-1) criterion**. This means that the failure of any one part, for example a line or a transformer, must not lead to a power cut. Hospitals and data centres have an **uninterruptible power supply** with batteries that steps in immediately. After a few seconds, emergency generators with diesel engines take over.

After a big outage you cannot simply switch everything on at the same time. First, power stations with **black start capability** start up; these need no electricity from the grid, for example hydroelectric power stations. Then the grid is rebuilt step by step and one area after another is connected again. With big outages, this can take many hours.

In Switzerland, the electricity industry’s organisation **OSTRAL** prepares measures in case there is ever too little electricity, for instance in winter. The federal government recommends that every household keeps an **emergency supply** of water, food and important things. These include a torch, spare batteries and a battery-powered radio through which the authorities can give information. You should only light candles under supervision and never near curtains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A widespread power cut that lasts a long time.
A chain reaction in which one failure triggers further failures.
A generator with an engine that produces electricity during a power cut.
Starting up a power station without electricity from the grid.

gewusst: Because Rome was celebrating the culture night Notte Bianca that very night, many people suddenly found themselves sitting in the dark in the middle of the city.
In a power cut, a fridge keeps food cool for a few more hours if you keep the door shut.

teile.einleitung: The power grid is a huge web of lines, substations and transformers that brings electricity from the power stations to every socket. It ranges from mighty high-voltage lines over the Alps to the cable under the road outside your house. For everything to work, production and consumption have to be exactly the same at every moment.
wichtigste: The power grid connects power stations with all consumers.
The Swiss power grid is divided into 7 grid levels.
Over long distances, electricity is transmitted at a very high voltage, because the losses are then smaller.
Transformers change the voltage, for example from high voltage to 230 volts.
The Swissgrid transmission network is about 6700 kilometres long.
In 1958, the grids of Germany, France and Switzerland were connected for the first time at Laufenburg in Aargau.
Production and consumption must always be the same so that the frequency stays stable.

abschnitte.text: Electricity is produced in power stations, for example in hydroelectric power stations in the Alps or in solar panels on roofs. Through the **power grid** it reaches factories, railways and households. Because electricity can hardly be stored, it has to be used at the very moment it is produced. So the grid is like a cycle that must never stop.

The Swiss grid is divided into **7 grid levels**. At the top is the **transmission network** with 380 000 and 220 000 volts, which transports large amounts of electricity across the country like a motorway. Below it come supra-regional and regional distribution networks, and at the very bottom the local network with 400 and 230 volts. In between are levels with substations, where the voltage is converted.

In every line, part of the energy is lost as heat. The higher the voltage, the smaller the current that has to flow for the same power, and the smaller the **losses**. That is why electricity is transported over long distances at high voltage. A **transformer** then steps the voltage down bit by bit until it is 230 volts at the socket.

The European power grid works at a **frequency** of 50 hertz. If more electricity is used than produced, the frequency falls; if more is produced, it rises. That is why power stations constantly have to adjust, so that production and consumption are exactly the same. If the balance is badly upset, there is a risk of a **blackout**, a widespread power cut that lasts a long time.

The Swiss transmission network belongs to the national grid company **Swissgrid** and is about 6700 kilometres long. Switzerland is closely connected with its neighbours and lies right in the middle of the European power network. It all began in 1958 with the so-called **Star of Laufenburg** in Aargau, where the grids of Germany, France and Switzerland were connected for the first time. This means the countries can help each other out when electricity is short somewhere.

More and more electricity comes from solar panels and wind turbines, which supply different amounts depending on the weather. That is why the grid is becoming more modern and digital; this is called a **smart grid**. An important building block is the **smart meter**, a digital electricity meter that sends the consumption data automatically. This way grid operators know better when how much electricity is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that raises or lowers the voltage of electricity.
A facility where electricity is converted from one voltage to another.
How often alternating current changes direction per second, measured in hertz.
A digital electricity meter that reports consumption automatically.

gewusst: The European interconnected grid links many countries from the Atlantic to the Black Sea and is one of the largest power grids in the world.
If you measure the frequency of the power grid precisely, you can tell from the value whether too much or too little electricity is being produced in Europe at that moment.

teile.einleitung: The Swatch is a plastic wristwatch that came onto the market in Switzerland in 1983. With bright colours, cheeky patterns and low prices, it became a cult object around the world. At the same time it helped the Swiss watch industry out of a severe crisis.
wichtigste: A Swatch is a wristwatch.
The first Swatch came out in 1983.
The case of the classic Swatch is made of plastic.
The name is made up of the English words Second and Watch.
The Swatch company has its headquarters in Biel.
Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch.
The Swatch was invented to help the Swiss watch industry.
The Swatch is known above all for its bright colours and patterns.

abschnitte.text: The Swatch is a **quartz watch** with a case made of **plastic**. It consists of only 51 individual parts, far fewer than traditional watches. The parts are assembled by machine and the case is welded shut instead of screwed. That is why the watch could be made cheaply in Switzerland.

In the 1970s, cheap **quartz watches** from Japan and Hong Kong came onto the market. Many Swiss watch companies could not compete with these prices. Tens of thousands of jobs were lost, especially in the Jura Arc. Today this hard time is called the **quartz crisis**.

Engineers at the company ETA in Grenchen, including Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller, developed a watch that could be made very cheaply. On 1 March 1983 the first Swatch was presented. The name comes from **Second Watch**, because people were meant to own several and change them depending on their mood. The watch was marketed like a fashion item.

The businessman **Nicolas G. Hayek** helped to reorganise the struggling Swiss watch companies. He brought them together in one large group, which today is called the **Swatch Group** and has its headquarters in **Biel**. It also includes well-known brands such as Omega, Longines and Tissot. That is why Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch and the saviour of the Swiss watch industry.

Every year, new Swatch models come out in bright **colours** and patterns. Many were designed by artists. Some rare models are now sought-after collector’s items and worth much more than when they were bought. In 2013 Swatch also brought out a mechanical watch with automatic winding, the Sistem51.

begriffe.erklaerung: A watch in which a vibrating quartz crystal measures the time precisely.
The severe crisis of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s.
An object that a great many people enthusiastically collect or wear.
The large Swiss watch group to which the Swatch brand belongs.

gewusst: The Sistem51 has this name because its mechanical movement also consists of only 51 parts.
Swatch’s new headquarters in Biel has a huge curving wooden roof that looks like a snake.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Light Source, SLS for short, is a large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Aargau. There, electrons circle in a ring at almost the speed of light and produce extremely bright X-ray light as they do so. With this light, researchers study materials, medicines and tiny structures.
wichtigste: The SLS has been in operation at the PSI since 2001.
Its storage ring has a circumference of 288 metres.
The X-ray light is produced when electrons are steered onto curved paths.
From 2023 to 2025 the storage ring was renewed in the SLS 2.0 upgrade.
According to the PSI, SLS 2.0 improves the emittance, that is how tightly the beam is bundled, by up to a factor of 40.
Pharmaceutical companies use the SLS especially for protein crystallography.
In top-up operation the ring is constantly refilled so that the current stays constant.
There are about 20 experiment stations at the SLS.

abschnitte.titel: What is a synchrotron light source?
abschnitte.text: In a synchrotron light source, **electrons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Then they circle in a large ring, the **storage ring**. Whenever magnets steer the electrons onto a curved path, they give off light. This **synchrotron light** ranges from infrared to hard X-rays and is much brighter than the light from an X-ray tube in hospital.

The SLS is in Villigen in the canton of Aargau and has been in operation since 2001. Its storage ring has a circumference of 288 metres and lies in a round building. Along about 20 **beamlines**, the light is led to experiment stations. In **top-up operation**, the ring is constantly refilled with small amounts of electrons so that the current, and therefore the brightness, stays the same.

An important area of use is **protein crystallography**. This is used to find out exactly how proteins made of millions of atoms are built. Pharmaceutical companies use this knowledge to develop suitable medicines. At the SLS, batteries, rocks, materials or even old works of art are also examined with X-rays without damaging them.

From 2023 to 2025 the storage ring was completely renewed in the **SLS 2.0** project. New magnets bundle the electron beam much more tightly. According to the PSI, the **emittance**, the measure of how well the beam is bundled, improves by up to a factor of 40. This makes the X-ray light even brighter and sharper, and experiments become faster and more precise.

The **Paul Scherrer Institute** is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. Besides the SLS, it runs other large facilities, such as the SwissFEL X-ray laser and a neutron source. Every year, researchers from many countries come to Villigen to carry out measurements at these facilities. The PSI lies on the River Aare and is part of the ETH Domain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ring-shaped tunnel in which electrons fly round in a circle for a long time.
Very bright light that electrons give off on curved paths.
A measure of how tightly the electron beam is bundled.
An important building block of all living things.

gewusst: The electrons in the SLS circle the 288-metre ring about a million times per second.
Synchrotron light was first discovered as an annoying side effect of particle accelerators, before special facilities were built for it.
